title: The Stable on West Street That Became Madam Walker's Factory
dek: In 1910 Madam C. J. Walker settled in Indianapolis, turned a stable behind her house into a factory and built a company around the women she trained.

story.company: Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company
story.event: Moving to Indianapolis, building a factory behind her West Street house and incorporating the company
story.summary: In February 1910 Madam C. J. Walker, who had sold her hair-care products door to door since 1906 and trained agents at a school in Pittsburgh, moved her base to Indianapolis. She bought a house at 640 North West Street, turned the stable and warehouse behind it into a factory and office, set up a laboratory and beauty school, and in September 1911 incorporated the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company, recruiting Alice Kelly to run the factory and Freeman B. Ransom as general manager.
paragraphs: In February 1910 Madam C. J. Walker moved to Indianapolis. She was 42, a former laundress who had spent the years since 1906 selling her Wonderful Hair Grower door to door, demonstrating scalp treatments in churches and lodges across the South and East, and, since 1908, training "hair culturists" at a school in Pittsburgh named after her daughter, Lelia. Indianapolis, her biographer notes, was then the country's largest inland manufacturing centre. The Indiana Historical Society says she chose it as her permanent base after a visit.

She was deciding what kind of business to build, and where. Her products reached customers through women she trained, and the agents' work, as the Historical Society's guide to her papers puts it, was not only to sell but to teach hygiene and pride in appearance. Very few kinds of work besides domestic service and manual labour were then open to Black women. She bought a house at 640 North West Street, turned the stable and warehouse behind it into a factory and office, and set up a laboratory and a beauty school.

She joined Bethel AME Church and the local business league. In September 1911 a young lawyer, Robert Brokenburr, drew up the papers incorporating the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company, with Walker, her daughter and her husband as directors. She recruited Alice Kelly, a former dean of girls at a Kentucky boarding school, to manage the factory, and persuaded Freeman B. Ransom, a lawyer who boarded at her house, to become general manager; he stayed until his death in 1947. Her $1,000 gift to the building fund of the city's Black YMCA made news in the Black press.

In 1912, snubbed by Booker T. Washington at the National Negro Business League convention in Chicago, she took the floor anyway, with the support of George Knox, editor of the Indianapolis Freeman. She told the delegates how she had come from the cotton fields to the washtub and the kitchen, and said: "I have built my own factory on my own ground." When she moved to New York in 1916, Ransom and Kelly ran the factory. By 1917 she claimed to have trained nearly 20,000 women; the Historical Society speaks of several thousand agents.

quote.text: There is some of the same fitness in a man’s building his own house that there is in a bird’s building its own nest.
quote.source_title: Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience, Project Gutenberg eBook #205
quote.connection: Thoreau saw a natural fitness in building your own shelter, as a bird builds its nest. Walker built her factory behind her own house, then trained thousands of other women to build trades of their own: work on their own ground, in her phrase.

reflection: Walker did not wait to be invited. When the most powerful man in the room would not call on her, she spoke about what she could point to: a factory, a school, women earning a living outside other people's kitchens.

You may sometimes feel unseen by people whose approval would make the work easier. It helps to know what your own ground is: the thing you have made that stays true whether or not anyone in authority notices it. Name it plainly, as she did. Then go back to tending it, and let that, not the room, decide how you feel about the day.
invitation: Write one plain sentence about something you have built, the way you would say it if someone gave you thirty seconds at a podium. Keep it somewhere you will see it this week.

sources.supports: Born Sarah Breedlove in Delta, Louisiana; worked as a laundress; Lelia College opened in Pittsburgh in 1908 to train agents and beauty culturists; arrival in Indianapolis in 1910; $1,000 gift to the Senate Avenue YMCA building fund; joined Bethel AME Church and the local National Negro Business League; bought 640 N. West Street and remodelled a stable and warehouse at the rear into a factory and office; Brokenburr drafted the articles of incorporation in 1911; recruited Alice Kelly, former dean of girls at a Kentucky boarding school, to manage the factory; persuaded Freeman B. Ransom to become general manager until his death in 1947; moved to New York in 1916 with Ransom and Kelly running the company; claimed by 1917 to have trained nearly 20,000 women

sources.title: About Madam C. J. Walker: A Brief Biographical Essay and FAQs (A'Lelia Bundles, 2020)
sources.supports: Born 23 December 1867; a year and a half of travel selling door to door and demonstrating treatments in churches and lodges; Lelia College in Pittsburgh from 1908; settled in Indianapolis by early 1910 (the FAQ gives February 1910), then the nation's largest inland manufacturing centre, building a factory, salon and training school; the $1,000 YMCA gift within a year of arrival; Walker's 1912 words, 'I have built my own factory on my own ground'; Ransom and Alice Kelly left in charge in 1916

sources.title: Madam C. J. Walker Papers, 1910-1980 (Collection M 0399), collection guide with biographical sketch

Walker as directors; several thousand agents; agents' role to educate customers in hygiene and appearance, not merely sell; few work outlets for Black women beyond domestic service and manual labour; Ransom boarded at her house; snubbed by Booker T. Washington, she took the podium at the 1912 National Negro Business League meeting in Chicago with George Knox's support; her denial in 1918 that she was a millionaire

research_notes: Sources are A'Lelia Bundles's biography-based writing (her Encyclopedia of Indianapolis entry and the official madamcjwalker.com essay and FAQs, both drawn from her biography On Her Own Ground) and the Indiana Historical Society, as the assignment asked. Agent numbers disagree widely: Bundles's entry says Walker claimed by 1917 to have trained nearly 20,000 women; the Indiana Historical Society speaks of several thousand agents; the National Women's History Museum's figure of 40,000 employees (from a page that also misdates her divorce to 1910) is not used. The story gives the first two with attribution. YMCA gift: Bundles says it came less than a year after her arrival; the Historical Society's exhibit page dates it to 1912; the story gives no date. Arrival: Bundles's FAQ says February 1910 and her essay 'by early 1910'; the Historical Society says 1910. The factory: Bundles says she remodelled a stable and warehouse behind the house; an Historical Society photograph record says that by 1911 the house itself served as home, office, salon and factory; the story uses Bundles's description. Her 1912 speech: the official site dates the quotation 'July 1912' and the Historical Society places it at the 1912 National Negro Business League meeting in Chicago, so the story says only 1912; the two sources word the opening lines slightly differently, and the story quotes only the closing sentence, which appears in the official site's text. The Historical Society's guide calls Knox 'Freedom publisher', evidently a slip for the Freeman, which its exhibit page names. Walker is often called the first self-made woman millionaire; the Historical Society notes she denied being a millionaire in a 1918 letter, and the story makes no wealth claim. The repeat screen may flag Maggie Lena Walker (a different person sharing the surname); the founder field is unchanged. Thoreau's passage argues for building one's own house; applied here by analogy.
